evidence.claim: Roads meet at a former pasture, then reach a knife-making village.
evidence.quote: It is the home of the former Northfield Knife Company

evidence.claim: Litchfield’s scenic roads meet at a green framed by a district of Georgian buildings with clapboard walls, gables and hipped roofs.
evidence.quote: This residential district is anchored by the Litchfield meetinghouse (1829) and is predominantly Georgian with clapboarding, gables and hipped roofs.

evidence.claim: Routes 202 and 63 cross at the green; Route 118 leaves eastward, crossing the Bantam River before meeting Route 254 toward Northfield.
evidence.quote: Route 118 begins at the corner of South Street and East Street in the Litchfield green at the center of the borough at an intersection with Route 63. It heads east as the southern branch of East Street, crosses the Bantam River, then intersects with Route 254 (the road to the village of Northfield).

evidence.claim: Connecticut designates scenic sections of Routes 118 and 254 here.
evidence.quote: The section of Route 254 from Camp Hill Road in the village of Northfield to the northern terminus in Litchfield borough is designated as a state scenic road.

evidence.claim: The eastward road has a turnpike ancestry: the Litchfield and Harwinton Turnpike company received its charter in 1798 to improve and maintain the connection through Litchfield, Harwinton and Burlington.
evidence.quote: The Litchfield and Harwinton Turnpike company was chartered in October 1798 to improve and maintain the road between the villages of Litchfield, Harwinton, and Burlington

evidence.claim: Its alignment used what is now Route 118.
evidence.quote: The turnpike used modern Route 118 then continued past Harwinton along modern Route 4 to the Avon town line.

evidence.claim: A later highway realignment left East Litchfield Road as the old alignment, and the present Route 118 number arrived in 1966.
evidence.quote: The old alignment is now East Litchfield Road. In 1963, Route 4 was relocated to its modern alignment and the east end of Route 116 was truncated to Harwinton. In 1966, Route 116 was renumbered to Route 118

evidence.claim: Approach the center from the Morris line on Route 63, then take Route 118 east from the green.

evidence.claim: At Route 254, the journey turns toward Northfield in southeastern Litchfield.
evidence.quote: In Litchfield, Route 254 soon enters the village of Northfield, then continues northwest for about 4.7 miles (7.6 km) to end at an intersection with Route 118 in the borough of Litchfield.

evidence.claim: There, Northfield Pond and Knife Shop Dam belong to Humaston Brook State Park, with the knife factory’s foundations surviving nearby.
evidence.quote: The foundations of the original knife factory still remain, and were listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1997. Both Northfield Pond and the Knife Shop Dam are part of Humaston Brook State Park.

evidence.claim: Routes 202 and 63 cross at the green
evidence.quote: At the center of the district is the Litchfield Town Green in the area of the intersection between Route 202 and Route 63

evidence.claim: Connecticut designates scenic sections of Routes 118 and 254 here.
evidence.quote: The 2.8-mile (4.5 km) section from the western terminus at the Litchfield green to the village of East Litchfield, and the 0.1-mile (0.16 km) section within the town center of Harwinton have both been designated by the state as scenic roads.

evidence.claim: At Route 254, the journey turns toward Northfield in southeastern Litchfield.
evidence.quote: The village of Northfield is located in the southeastern corner of Litchfield.

evidence.claim: Legal education here outgrew a downstairs parlor.
evidence.quote: Students lived in the homes of town residents and traveled to Reeve's house on South Street to receive their morning lectures on the common law in Reeve's downstairs parlor.

evidence.claim: Tapping Reeve began teaching in 1774; rising demand led him to build a separate, one-room school beside his South Street house in 1784.
evidence.quote: Reeve began teaching his first student in 1774, and by 1784 was teaching by lecture.

evidence.claim: Students lodged with town residents and came to the house for morning lectures on common law.
evidence.quote: Students lived in the homes of town residents and traveled to Reeve's house on South Street to receive their morning lectures on the common law in Reeve's downstairs parlor.

evidence.claim: Before closing in 1833, the school educated more than 1,100 students, including Aaron Burr and John C. Calhoun.
evidence.quote: The school closed in 1833, having educated over 1,100 students, including Aaron Burr and John C. Calhoun.

evidence.claim: The Litchfield Historical Society operates the house and school as a museum of nineteenth-century school life.
evidence.quote: which is owned and operated by the Litchfield Historical Society as a museum displaying life in a 19th-century period school.

evidence.claim: rising demand led him to build a separate, one-room school beside his South Street house in 1784.
evidence.quote: In 1784, in response to increasing demand, Reeve had a one-room school built adjacent to his house.

evidence.claim: The town green began as shared pasture in 1720, with a meetinghouse added in 1723.
evidence.quote: The village green was originally established in 1720 and was primarily used as a common pasture ground, in addition to being the site of the first town meetinghouse, which was constructed in 1723.

evidence.claim: A schoolhouse followed in 1732, then a courthouse in 1751 as Litchfield became the new county’s seat.
evidence.quote: including the first schoolhouse in the area in 1732, and the county courthouse in 1751, when Litchfield became the county seat of newly constituted Litchfield County.

evidence.claim: After the Revolution, grazing gave way to military parades; in 1836 the town designated the green as a park.
evidence.quote: The use of the green as pasture ceased after the Revolutionary War and became used as a military parade ground. Its transformation into a park began in 1836, when it was officially designated by the town as such.

evidence.claim: The meetinghouse anchoring the historic district dates to 1829, a later building than the green’s first meetinghouse.
evidence.quote: This residential district is anchored by the Litchfield meetinghouse (1829)

evidence.claim: Clapboard walls, gables and hipped roofs define the district’s predominantly Georgian architecture.
evidence.quote: is predominantly Georgian with clapboarding, gables and hipped roofs.

evidence.claim: Knife Shop Dam began with another trade: carriage making.
evidence.quote: Humaston Brook was dammed in 1854 to provide water power to a carriage manufacturer.

evidence.claim: Humaston Brook was dammed for that work in 1854, and J. Howard Catlin and his brother Franklin bought the factory and water rights in 1858 for their knife company.
evidence.quote: Humaston Brook was dammed in 1854 to provide water power to a carriage manufacturer. J. Howard Catlin purchased the factory and its water rights in 1858 with his brother Franklin as a site for their knife company.

evidence.claim: The Northfield Knife Company operated until 1926.
evidence.quote: the former Northfield Knife Company, which was founded in 1858 and ceased operations in 1926.

evidence.claim: Its foundations remain below the dam in Humaston Brook State Park.
evidence.quote: It also includes the foundations of the former Northfield Knife Company located along the banks of the brook below the dam

evidence.claim: A trail south of Knife Shop Road reaches the factory ruins and cascades, placing the remains of manufacturing beside the brook that supplied its water power.
evidence.quote: A hiking trail provides access to the cascades and factory ruins south of Knife Shop Road.

evidence.claim: The Route 118 scenic section extends 2.8 miles from the green toward East Litchfield; Route 254’s designated stretch reaches Camp Hill Road in Northfield.
evidence.quote: The 2.8-mile (4.5 km) section from the western terminus at the Litchfield green to the village of East Litchfield

evidence.claim: Route 254’s designated stretch reaches Camp Hill Road in Northfield.
evidence.quote: The section of Route 254 from Camp Hill Road in the village of Northfield to the northern terminus in Litchfield borough is designated as a state scenic road.

evidence.claim: The Thomaston-Northfield-Litchfield road acquired the Route 254 number in 1963, replacing its earlier unsigned state-road designation.
evidence.quote: Prior to 1963, the Thomaston-Northfield-Litchfield road was an unsigned state highway designated as State Road 854. As part of the 1962 Route Reclassification Act, SR 854 was renumbered to Route 254 at the beginning of 1963.

evidence.claim: Lectures ranged across property, contracts, evidence and crimes, covering the whole body of law.
evidence.quote: The school's lectures covered the entire body of the law including real estate, rights of persons, rights of things, contracts, torts, evidence, pleading, crimes, and equity.

evidence.claim: During the Civil War, the green served as a recruiting center and a place to welcome returning soldiers.
evidence.quote: The green was used as the center for recruitment during the Civil War and was also the place returning soldiers were welcomed.

evidence.claim: The company’s knives appeared at world fairs between 1876 and 1901, reaching beyond the village where they were made.
evidence.quote: The company became one of the nation's leading manufacturers of knives, its wares displayed at various world fairs between 1876 and 1901.
